memories.content: Link expected participant burden in each user study task to its corresponding mitigation strategy.
Specify the accommodations necessary for participants to access the prototype and research tasks.
Specify how accessibility accommodations will be provided during user study sessions.
Describe how personal identifiers will be separated from research data immediately after collection.
Specify the equipment to be loaned to participants who lack necessary devices.
Describe the procedure for returning equipment loaned to participants.
HCI ethics reviewers verify that expected burdens and mitigation strategies correspond to each user study task.
Inform participants that the formative evaluation prototype is not a finished service.
Set an upper limit on cumulative task burden when requesting repeated evaluations from the same participant.
The author of this proposal tends to emphasize expected benefits of the prototype over participant burden.
In organizations where leaders or institutional staff handle recruitment, recruitment authority and academic or professional evaluation authority may be combined in the same role.
Calculate user research compensation budgets based on the estimated participation burden, combining session time with required technical and travel preparation.
Compensate participants who withdraw from the study midway for their actual participation time.
Compensate for the time actually spent in sessions, regardless of the research modality.
Allow the issuance of gift cards of equivalent value to participants in remote studies who cannot use electronic transfers.
Do not treat an unresolved payment method as a deficiency at the proposal stage.
Allow differential compensation amounts for on-site and remote studies when participation burden varies due to travel or technical preparation.
Participants judge the fairness of compensation based on the combined burden of session time and required technical and travel preparation.
In longitudinal studies requiring diary entries and repeated reporting, include out-of-session recording time in compensation calculations.
Distinguish between participant research compensation and labor costs for field staff performing installation and operational support as part of their duties.
The user tends to count session time but omit participants’ advance setup and follow-up reporting time.

analysis.overview: Both frames center participant burden, but apply it differently: one links task burden to mitigation, while the other uses burden to set compensation. The remaining material covers separate ethics, accessibility, data, equipment, recruitment, payment, and workload safeguards.

relations.reason: The claims share a burden-responsive study-planning principle, while their explicit operational scopes—mitigation per task versus compensation reflecting session, travel, and technical preparation—must be preserved.
relations.summary: Both frames require participant burden to shape study protections, with the reference applying it to task-level mitigation and the compared frame applying it to compensation budgets and modality-sensitive amounts.

relations.reason: These memories split the requirements and delivery aspects of one one-sided accessibility-planning claim, with no corresponding compared-frame claim.
relations.summary: The reference requires identifying necessary accessibility accommodations and specifying how they will be delivered during study sessions.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful one-sided data-protection requirement.
relations.summary: The reference requires personal identifiers to be separated from research data immediately after collection.

relations.reason: These memories split the provision and return stages of one one-sided equipment-lending policy.
relations.summary: The reference requires specifying both equipment loans for participants lacking devices and the procedure for returning that equipment.

relations.reason: Reviewer verification is a distinct governance safeguard not stated in the compared frame.
relations.summary: The reference assigns ethics reviewers responsibility for checking that each study task's burden corresponds to its mitigation.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful one-sided disclosure requirement.
relations.summary: The reference requires participants to be told that the formative prototype is not a finished service.

relations.reason: This is a distinct repeated-participation safeguard; the compared frame's longitudinal compensation rule does not impose a burden limit.
relations.summary: The reference requires an upper limit on cumulative task burden for participants asked to complete repeated evaluations.

relations.reason: This is a one-sided diagnostic about benefit framing, not the compared frame's narrower omission of particular time burdens.
relations.summary: The reference identifies a tendency by the proposal author to emphasize prototype benefits over participant burden.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful one-sided observation about concentrated institutional authority.
relations.summary: The reference notes that recruitment authority and academic or professional evaluation authority may be combined when organizational leaders or staff recruit participants.

relations.reason: These memories state the general actual-time payment rule and its withdrawal application as one one-sided compensation claim.
relations.summary: The compared frame requires compensation for actual session participation time across modalities, including when a participant withdraws midway.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful one-sided payment-method accommodation.
relations.summary: The compared frame permits equivalent-value gift cards for remote participants unable to use electronic transfers.

relations.reason: This is a distinct one-sided review-stage policy, separate from authorizing any particular payment alternative.
relations.summary: The compared frame says an unresolved payment method should not be treated as a proposal-stage deficiency.

relations.reason: This one-sided claim describes the participant fairness standard supporting burden-inclusive compensation.
relations.summary: The compared frame states that participants assess compensation fairness using session time together with required technical and travel preparation.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful one-sided rule for a specific workload outside study sessions.
relations.summary: The compared frame requires out-of-session diary and repeated-reporting time to be included in longitudinal-study compensation calculations.

relations.reason: This is an independently useful one-sided cost-classification rule.
relations.summary: The compared frame distinguishes participant research compensation from labor costs for field staff performing installation and operational support as job duties.

relations.reason: This is a one-sided diagnostic about incomplete time accounting, distinct from the reference frame's broader benefit-over-burden framing tendency.
relations.summary: The compared frame identifies a tendency to count session time while omitting participants' advance setup and follow-up reporting time.

reports.compared_only: The compared frame adds actual-time payment, payment-method flexibility, fairness criteria, longitudinal reporting time, staff-cost separation, and a setup-time omission bias.
reports.differences: Participant burden drives task-level mitigation in the reference frame, but compensation budgeting and modality-based amounts in the compared frame.
reports.reference_only: The reference adds accessibility delivery, data separation, equipment lending, ethics review, prototype disclosure, cumulative-burden limits, benefit-framing bias, and recruitment-authority risk.
